content: Okay, checking in from the restaurant. It's just past nine and the second seating is winding down, so I've got a window to talk. Nakajima is still in the kitchen running things and so far it's been a genuinely solid week — I want to give you the full mid-service picture on how he's been doing holding the pass while Marco is in Modena. But I also need to tell you about something that happened tonight that I was completely not expecting, and I want to think through it with you before the adrenaline of the situation wears off and I either over-react or under-react. Both of those are possible for me when I'm tired and the service hasn't fully closed yet.

Good timing for a check-in — mid-service or just-past-second-seating is usually when you get the most honest read of how a week is actually going, before the post-close fatigue smooths everything into a blur. Start with Nakajima and the kitchen, because that's the foundation everything else sits on. Tell me specifically how he's been holding the pass: not just whether it's gone well in a general sense, but what the actual numbers look like, whether you're seeing any cracks in his communication with the floor team, and whether he's been leaning on you more than you expected or less. I want to understand if this week has been a steady performance or whether it's been more uneven — some nights strong, some nights where you could feel the seams showing. Then tell me what the unexpected thing is. I'm guessing from the way you're framing it that it's not a kitchen crisis or a staffing problem, but I don't want to assume and get ahead of you.

Nakajima is holding up well — that's my honest read after four days of him running the kitchen while Marco is away. I was genuinely nervous coming into this week because taking the pass at Osteria Morishita is a different kind of pressure than running a section of the kitchen. You're not just cooking anymore. You're reading the entire floor simultaneously, timing six or seven tables at once, and you're the person Sawada is going to come to every time anything goes sideways between the kitchen and the floor. Nakajima has historically gone quiet when he's stressed, which is exactly the wrong response at the pass, and I expected that to show up under this level of sustained pressure. But it hasn't. He's been verbally sharp, he's calling the kitchen clearly, and the ticket times are actually solid. We're sitting at 24 minutes average for dinner across the week, which is only about two minutes off what we run when Marco is here. I was expecting a five or six minute slip at a minimum given that Nakajima has never done a full week at this level of responsibility before. So on the pure metrics side, I'm genuinely pleased with where things stand. Eiko actually told me after the first seating tonight that she feels like the handoff between kitchen and floor has been smoother this week than it sometimes is with Marco, which I thought was a very interesting thing for her to say. I took it as a real compliment to Nakajima rather than as any kind of knock on Marco — their styles are genuinely different, and maybe for this particular week Eiko is responding well to the predictability that Nakajima's approach creates. Anyway, that's the background. The unexpected thing is the thing I really need to talk through.

24 minutes average for dinner tickets with Nakajima running the pass solo is a number worth pausing on for a moment, because two minutes of slip from your Marco-present baseline is well within the range of normal night-to-night variation. You'd expect more variance than that just from the natural differences in how tables order and how quickly guests move through courses on any given evening. The fact that he's holding to that standard while also managing all the coordination work — reading the floor, calling the kitchen, fielding Sawada's questions in real time — tells you something important about where he actually is developmentally versus where you might have estimated him to be. A lot of cooks who are technically excellent at their station come apart at the pass because the pass isn't a cooking job, it's a traffic management and communication job, and Nakajima's history of going quiet under stress is exactly the kind of temperamental pattern that kills pass performance. The fact that he's overriding that tendency under sustained pressure rather than a one-off busy night is meaningful. Eiko's observation about the kitchen-floor handoff is also worth taking seriously rather than discounting as politeness. She's reading that interface every single service from the floor side, and her calibration on what smooth versus rough handoff actually feels like is better than almost anyone else in the building. The contrast she's drawing between Marco's improvisational style and Nakajima's more methodical approach is real, and it has practical consequences: improvisation at the pass creates flexibility but also variance, and some floor teams find predictable rhythm easier to work against than brilliance that they can't anticipate. Neither style is categorically better, but in a restaurant at Osteria Morishita's level, there are nights where Nakajima's approach produces fewer interruptions to the guest experience even if Marco's ceiling on his best nights is higher. Now — tell me about the unexpected thing, because something in how you're holding back on it tells me it matters.

Around seven-fifteen tonight, Sawada came to find me in the office — I was between the seatings working through some supplier invoices — and she told me that a woman who had just been seated at table eleven was someone she was fairly certain was Hiroko Sano. The restaurant critic from Asahi Shimbun Weekly. Sano did not announce herself, she just came in through the normal reservations process, made the booking under a different name, and sat down. But Sawada recognized her from a panel event she attended last year and was confident enough in the identification that she wanted to flag it immediately rather than wait. So I had about thirty seconds to decide how to respond to that information before the window to do anything useful was going to close. The decision I made was: we do not change anything visible. No sending over an amuse-bouche that we don't send to other tables, no extra pass from me to table eleven, none of that. The reasoning was exactly what you'd expect — if Sano is trying to get an honest read of what we actually deliver to a normal guest, me performing for her is going to undermine the restaurant's credibility if she notices it, and critics at her level notice it. What I did instead was go directly to the kitchen and tell Nakajima that we had a guest tonight who might be doing a review, and that I wanted him to treat that as a signal to be at his absolute sharpest for every table in the room, not just for one. I framed it as general excellence rather than 'there's a VIP at eleven' — I wanted him to elevate the whole room without fixating on a single cover. Then I came back to the floor and let service run.

The decision you made in that thirty seconds is the right one, and the reasoning you applied is exactly correct on every point. When a critic of Sano's caliber comes in without announcing herself — when Sano did not announce herself but Sawada recognized her at the restaurant — the entire point of that choice is to see what a real guest experiences, not what a restaurant performs on command. Critics who have been doing this long enough have developed a very precise instinct for the tells: an unexpected amuse-bouche arriving before they've had time to establish whether they want it, an owner who appears at their table with just a little too much warmth, a kitchen whose pacing suddenly shifts in a way that doesn't match the rhythm of the room. Any one of those signals would have flagged to Sano that her cover was blown, and the article that comes from a detected critic visit reads differently — sometimes subtly, sometimes not subtly at all — from one that comes from a genuinely anonymous experience. The briefing to Nakajima was constructed well. 'There's a guest tonight who might be reviewing us — I want the whole room at its best' is a completely different communication than 'VIP at table eleven, handle accordingly.' The first one raises the baseline for every cover. The second one creates exactly the visible differential that you were trying to avoid, and it also introduces the kind of tension into a kitchen mid-service that can actually degrade performance rather than sharpen it. How did the service go from that point forward? What was the state of table eleven when you last had information about it, and how did Nakajima respond to the briefing — did you see any visible change in the kitchen's behavior afterward?

The service went well. Sano ordered the tasting menu, which matters because that's the version of our cooking that most fully represents what we're trying to do — someone ordering à la carte is sampling individual dishes, but someone taking the full tasting menu is asking to be shown the restaurant's complete statement about food and hospitality. The progression, the pacing, the way each course sets up the next, the wine pairings, everything. She ordered a glass of the Vernaccia di San Gimignano with the first two courses and then moved to a glass of Barolo with the later savory courses. Eiko handled both of those wine conversations without any issues. I checked in with Eiko about thirty minutes after Sano was seated and she said the table seemed comfortable and engaged — Sano was eating everything, taking her time, and Eiko noticed she was writing notes between courses. As of about fifteen minutes ago table eleven had received all seven courses and Sano was finishing dessert. She left about twenty minutes ago without saying anything to the staff, which I expected. The thing that struck me when I walked through the kitchen during the service was that Nakajima was plating the fifth course himself rather than delegating the finish to one of the line cooks, which is something Marco does for important covers — but Nakajima was doing it without being told, and he wasn't doing it exclusively for table eleven. He was personally finishing the plating on that course for three or four tables around the same time. So he was responding to the heightened stakes of the evening in exactly the right way, which is to apply more care across the whole room rather than making it about one table.

Sano choosing the tasting menu is a significant piece of information about the intent behind the visit. A critic who comes in for a quick assessment of a specific dish orders à la carte and gets what she needs in ninety minutes. A critic who sits down for a full tasting menu is committing to understanding the restaurant's complete argument — what it believes food should do, how it thinks about a meal's arc, whether the hospitality holds up across the full length of an evening rather than just during the excitement of the first two courses. That's a deeper kind of evaluation, and it means the article, if there is one, will have more to say than a capsule review. The wine choices are telling in their own right: Vernaccia di San Gimignano into Barolo is the selection of someone who has thought about what these courses are doing and is pairing to the food rather than ordering by reputation or price. Eiko reading that correctly and handling both conversations well is a non-trivial contribution to how the evening was experienced. The note-taking between courses confirms what you already suspected: this is a working visit. She came to assess and record, not just to eat. Nakajima taking the plating of the fifth course himself — and doing it across multiple tables rather than only for table eleven — is exactly the right instinct expressed in exactly the right way. He's applying care at the point where it matters most without creating a visible signal that something unusual is happening. A less experienced cook running the pass for the first time would either have missed the moment entirely or over-corrected by fixating on one cover in a way the whole kitchen would have felt. Nakajima did neither. That's not just competence under pressure — it's judgment about what the situation actually requires, which is the harder thing to develop. Now: there's a question of what comes after tonight, and I suspect that's where your thinking is most active right now. The Sano visit doesn't end when she leaves the restaurant. What's the landscape you're navigating from here?

That's exactly what I need to think through. The first thing that's on my mind is the Tabelog context, because that's going to shape how new guests arrive at the restaurant if any article gets published. We're currently sitting at a 3.61 rating after 24 reviews, which for a restaurant that opened fourteen months ago in Higashi-Azabu is a reasonable position but not where I want to be long-term. We're in a neighborhood where the competitive baseline is high — there are a lot of restaurants in the three-something range and the ones that feel like genuine destinations rather than neighborhood options are the ones sitting in the high 3.6s and 3.7s. If Sano writes a piece for Asahi Shimbun Weekly, the readership is exactly the kind of audience that checks Tabelog before making a reservation, and the reviews that come in on the back of that exposure are going to have a meaningful effect on where the rating goes. I need the restaurant to be demonstrably excellent during the period when those new guests are showing up and potentially leaving reviews, not just during the night Sano herself was here. The second thing I'm thinking about is timing. I asked Eiko to try to pick up anything she could about when the piece might run, and from something Sano said near the end of the meal, the sense Eiko got was that the article publication is expected late March. Which means I have Marco back — he returns on March third — and then roughly three weeks between his return and the article dropping, assuming that timing is right. That's a meaningful window if I use it correctly. And the third thing is whether there's any appropriate way to contact Sano before publication, which my instinct says there isn't, but I want to think it through rather than just defaulting to inaction.

Let me work through all three of those in order, because they each have a different logic. On the Tabelog situation: the 3.61 after 24 reviews is a rating that is still fundamentally in formation. At 24 reviews, the statistical weight of each new review is high — a run of five or six detailed, thoughtful reviews from engaged diners can move that number meaningfully in either direction within a fairly short window. That's the vulnerability heading into a post-publication period, but it's also the opportunity. The readership of Asahi Shimbun Weekly is not a mass-market audience; it's an audience of people who think carefully about where they eat and who tend to leave the kind of detailed, scored reviews on Tabelog that carry more weight in the rating calculation than a one-sentence note. If the article is positive and the restaurant delivers on the experience it describes, the reviews that accumulate in the weeks after publication are likely to be quality reviews rather than just volume reviews, which is the better scenario for a sustained move toward 3.7 territory. The practical implication is that the four weeks after publication are a window you need to treat with essentially the same care as the night Sano was in the room. On the timing: article publication expected late March, with Marco back on March third. That's roughly a three-week window of full-strength kitchen before the exposure hits, which is genuinely workable. The most important thing you can do in that window is make sure the tasting menu that Sano experienced tonight is stable and well-executed when the first wave of new guests arrives, rather than in a state of revision. Marco will come back from Modena with ideas — he always does — and the case you'll need to make to him is that any significant menu changes should be held until April so you're not introducing new dishes right when expectant guests are showing up based on what a review describes. He'll push back, but he'll understand the logic if you frame it as protecting a window rather than suppressing his creativity. On contacting Sano: don't. The reasoning is the asymmetry of outcomes. If the article is positive, nothing you could do by reaching out improves the situation — the article says what it says, and reaching out before it publishes creates only risk without upside. If the article is mixed or includes a specific criticism, reaching out beforehand looks like you were attempting to influence the coverage, which is a worse outcome than the criticism itself. The right posture is exactly what you've been doing since seven-fifteen: let the work speak, make the restaurant excellent, and wait.

All of that maps to where I was landing intuitively, so it's useful to hear it confirmed with the reasoning made explicit. The one thing I want to add on the post-publication period is that I'm going to think carefully about Yuki's scheduling in March. She's one of our part-time servers and she tends to be stronger on her early shifts than her late ones when the weeks are long — it's a stamina and energy thing rather than a skill thing, and on a normal week it's not something that matters much. But if we're going to have a surge of more discerning guests who are showing up specifically because of what a review says, I want every element of the floor team to be at its best during that window, and Yuki's scheduling is a variable I can actually control. I can build her calendar in March so her shifts are weighted toward the earlier part of the week and the earlier seatings. Beyond that, I feel like I know what I'm doing. The bigger thing I want to think through before I close out tonight is how I'm going to handle the conversation with Nakajima. Because whatever the Sano article turns out to be, and whatever happens to the Tabelog rating over the next couple of months, tonight was a real moment for him personally and professionally. He ran dinner service at this restaurant during a visit by one of the more serious critics in the Tokyo restaurant press, he didn't know it for most of the night, and by every measure I have access to he delivered. I need to think about how to tell him that and when.

The Yuki scheduling observation is exactly the kind of specific, controllable variable that gets lost when you're thinking at the level of 'make the restaurant excellent for the post-publication window.' Macro intentions don't protect against micro gaps — and a floor team member who's running on low energy during a late Saturday seating in late March, when a guest who came specifically because of Sano's article is evaluating whether the review was accurate, is exactly the kind of gap that generates a muted Tabelog review rather than an enthusiastic one. Building her schedule around her known performance pattern during that window is smart staffing, not over-managing. On Nakajima: the question of how you tell him is important, and I think the how matters as much as the what. The factual content is straightforward — he ran a service tonight that included a visit from Hiroko Sano from Asahi Shimbun Weekly, the article publication is expected late March, the 24 minutes average ticket time held through that service, and you observed him making the right calls under pressure without being instructed to. Those are the specific things you want him to hear, because specific feedback is what a person can actually learn from and carry forward. But the framing around those facts is where you shape what the conversation does for him. This is not a reward conversation — 'you did well, here's a gold star.' It's a development conversation that happens to contain very positive evidence. The distinction matters because what Nakajima needs to understand is not just that he performed well tonight, but what specifically he did that constituted good performance, why those things mattered in the context of a service of this stakes level, and what it means for how Marco and you are going to think about his development going forward. The point about making sure Marco knows the full picture when he returns from Modena is also worth including in the conversation with Nakajima tonight — not as a political statement, but because Nakajima deserves to know that this week is on record in a concrete way, that it's going to inform how Marco structures his next phase of development rather than disappearing into a week that happened while Marco was away and therefore doesn't fully count.

That framing helps. I want to be specific rather than vague — I can tell him about the 24 minutes average on ticket times, I can tell him what I observed when I walked through the kitchen, I can tell him what Eiko said about the floor-kitchen handoff, and I can tell him about Sano and what I think tonight meant in context. I'm going to do it tonight, after the kitchen is cleaned down and the line cooks have gone. I want to give it the weight it deserves rather than squeezing it into the middle of the close when everyone's still moving. And yes, when Marco is back, I'll make sure he has the full account of this week before he and Nakajima get back into their normal working rhythm. Not as a political move — as information that Marco needs to develop Nakajima correctly from here. I feel settled on all of this now. The restaurant is in a good place tonight. Table eleven cleared cleanly, Eiko has the last two tables handled, Nakajima is doing breakdown in the kitchen. I should probably get back out there in the next few minutes.

You're in a good position heading into the close. To put the whole night in one place before you go: Nakajima held 24 minutes average on dinner tickets across a week where he was running the pass without Marco, demonstrated judgment under the pressure of a Sano visit he didn't fully know about, and made the right call at the plating station without being told what to do. Sawada recognized Hiroko Sano early enough that you could shape the response before it became reactive, and you made the disciplined choice not to perform for one table when the right move was to raise the entire room. Eiko executed her piece of the evening — the wine conversations, the floor-kitchen handoff, the quiet monitoring of table eleven — without a visible mistake. The article publication is expected late March, which gives you Marco's full return window to stabilize the tasting menu, position the floor staffing correctly, and make sure the restaurant is what it needs to be when guests start arriving based on what that article says. And tonight you tell Nakajima what the week actually was, in specific terms that he can carry forward. That's a clean set of outcomes for a February night when a Hiroko Sano from Asahi Shimbun Weekly walked in off the reservation list without announcing herself. Go close the service. The rest of this plays out over the next several weeks, and it's in good shape.
